lessons.title: Why Tomato Products Spoil: Mould, Yeast, and Bacteria
lessons.body: Tomato paste and sauce spoil because tiny organismsâmoulds, yeasts, and bacteriaâfeed on the sugars and acids in the product. These microbes are everywhere: in the air, on your hands, on utensils, and on the tomatoes themselves. When you cook tomatoes into paste or sauce, you kill many microbes, but the product becomes an ideal home for any that survive or get in later. Moulds appear as fuzzy green, white, or black spots. They grow best when there is air and some moisture. Yeasts cause fermentationâyou might see bubbles, smell alcohol or vinegar, and notice a sour taste. Bacteria can be dangerous; they may not change the look or smell but can cause food poisoning. The main culprits in tomato products are moulds like Aspergillus and Penicillium, yeasts like Saccharomyces, and bacteria such as Lactobacillus and Clostridium. Spoilage happens faster in warm, humid conditions. In many parts of Africa, temperatures above 30Â°C and high humidity make spoilage very rapid. A jar of tomato sauce left open in a hot kitchen can grow mould within 2â3 days. To slow spoilage, you must control four things: heat, acidity, moisture, and oxygen. Proper cooking kills microbes; adding acid (like lemon juice or vinegar) makes the environment too sour for many microbes; reducing water (by cooking down) makes it harder for them to grow; and sealing out air prevents moulds. Without these controls, your product may last only a few days. With them, it can last months. Understanding these enemies is the first step to defeating them.

lessons.title: Using Heat Processing to Extend Shelf Life
lessons.body: Heat processing is the most reliable way to extend the shelf life of tomato paste and sauce. The goal is to kill spoilage organisms and then seal the product so new ones cannot enter. For home or small-scale production, you can use a large pot for boiling water processing. First, fill clean glass jars with hot tomato product, leaving 1â2 cm of headspace. Wipe the rims, place lids on, and tighten them finger-tight. Then put the jars in a pot with a rack at the bottom. Add water until it covers the jars by 2â3 cm. Bring to a rolling boil and process for 35â45 minutes for pint (500 ml) jars, or 45â55 minutes for quart (1 litre) jars. At higher altitudes, add 5 minutes for every 300 metres above sea level. After processing, remove jars carefully and let them cool undisturbed for 12â24 hours. You should hear a âpopâ as the lids seal. To test the seal, press the centre of the lidâit should be firm and not move. If it pops back, the jar did not seal; refrigerate it and use within a week. For tomato paste, which is thicker and less acidic, you may need to add lemon juice or vinegar before processing to ensure safety. Alternatively, you can use a pressure canner, which reaches 121Â°C and kills all bacteria, including Clostridium botulinum. But pressure canners are expensive and not common in many African homes. Boiling water processing is more accessible. Always use clean, sterilised jars: boil them in water for 10 minutes before filling. Heat processing can give your tomato sauce a shelf life of 12â18 months if stored properly in a cool, dark place. Without heat processing, even refrigerated sauce may last only 1â2 weeks.

lessons.title: Natural Preservatives: Lemon Juice, Vinegar, and Salt
lessons.body: You donât need artificial preservatives to make tomato products last longer. Lemon juice, vinegar, and salt are natural preservatives that have been used for generations. They work by making the environment too acidic or too salty for moulds, yeasts, and bacteria to grow. Lemon juice and vinegar both contain acid. The acid lowers the pH of the tomato product. Most spoilage organisms cannot grow below pH 4.6. Tomatoes are naturally acidic, but not always enough. To be safe, add 1 tablespoon of bottled lemon juice (not fresh, because its acidity varies) per 500 ml of tomato sauce or paste. For vinegar, use 5% acidity white vinegar: add 2 tablespoons per 500 ml. Mix well and tasteâyou can adjust slightly, but donât reduce the acid if you want shelf stability. Salt also helps. It draws water out of microbes, killing them or slowing their growth. For tomato paste, add 1â2 teaspoons of salt per 500 g. For sauce, 1 teaspoon per 500 ml. But be careful: too much salt makes the product unpleasant, and salt alone does not prevent all spoilage. It works best combined with acid and heat. Another natural preservative is sugar in high concentrations, but that changes the flavour and is not typical for tomato products. You can also add a small amount of ascorbic acid (vitamin C) to prevent browning and boost acidity. Always use clean utensils when adding these preservatives. After adding, cook the product for at least 10 minutes to blend flavours and help the preservatives penetrate. Then process in a hot water bath as described in Lesson 2. With the right balance of lemon juice, vinegar, and salt, your tomato paste can last up to 12 months in a sealed jar, and your sauce up to 9 months. Without them, spoilage is much faster.

lessons.title: Proper Cooling and Storage After Opening
lessons.body: Once you open a jar of tomato paste or sauce, the clock starts ticking. Air, moisture, and microbes get in, and spoilage begins. Proper cooling and storage after opening can give you an extra 5â7 days in the refrigerator, or longer if you take extra steps. First, never leave an open jar at room temperature for more than 2 hours. If the room is above 30Â°C, that drops to 1 hour. After using what you need, immediately cover the jar and put it in the refrigerator. The fridge should be at 4Â°C or below. If you donât have a fridge, you can keep the jar in a cool, dark placeâlike a clay pot with a wet cloth around itâbut it will only last 1â2 days. For longer storage, you can freeze the paste or sauce. Spoon leftovers into ice cube trays or small plastic bags, freeze, and then transfer cubes to a freezer bag. Frozen tomato paste keeps for 3â6 months. When you want to use it, thaw only what you need. Reheating is important: bring the product to a rolling boil for at least 1 minute before eating, to kill any microbes that may have grown. Also, always use a clean spoon to take out the productânever double-dip. If you see any mould, smell something off, or notice bubbles, throw the whole jar away. Do not try to scrape off the mould; the roots may already be deep in the product. For long-term storage of opened jars, you can re-process them by heating the contents to boiling and putting them into a new sterilised jar, then processing in a hot water bath for 20 minutes. But this only works if the product is not already spoiled. Remember: refrigeration slows spoilage but does not stop it. Even in the fridge, use opened tomato paste within 5â7 days and sauce within 7â10 days for best quality.

lessons.title: Testing Shelf Life Without a Laboratory
lessons.body: You donât need a laboratory to know if your tomato paste or sauce is still good. You can do simple tests at home or in your shop. These tests rely on your senses and a few basic tools. First, the look test: check for mouldâfuzzy patches of green, white, black, or blue. Also look for gas bubbles, which mean fermentation. If the product looks swollen or the lid is bulging, throw it away. Second, the smell test: open the jar and sniff. Fresh tomato paste smells sweet and tangy. If it smells like alcohol, vinegar, or rot, itâs spoiled. Third, the taste test (only if it passes look and smell): take a tiny amount on a clean spoon and taste. If itâs fizzy, sour beyond normal, or bitter, spit it out and discard the jar. Fourth, the texture test: spoilage can make the product slimy or watery. If it has changed from its normal thick consistency, be suspicious. For a more scientific approach, you can measure pH with inexpensive pH strips (available at pharmacies or online). Tomato products should have a pH of 4.6 or lower for safe storage. If the pH is above 4.6, it is not safe for shelf storage and must be refrigerated and used quickly. You can also do a âspoon testâ: put a spoonful in a clear glass, cover, and leave at room temperature for 24 hours. If bubbles appear or it smells bad, spoilage is active. Another method is the âfloat testâ for jars: if a jar lid is convex (bulging up), itâs a sign of gas-producing bacteria. Always trust your senses. If in doubt, throw it out. Itâs better to lose a jar than to get sick. Record the date you made each batch and test a jar every month to learn how long your product lasts under your conditions.

lessons.title: Reducing Spoilage During Transport and Display
lessons.body: Transporting and displaying tomato paste and sauce in African markets can be tough on shelf life. Heat, sunlight, jostling, and humidity all speed up spoilage. To reduce spoilage, start with good packaging. Glass jars are best because they donât react with acid and seal tightly. Plastic containers can work if they are food-grade and have tight lids, but they may allow oxygen in over time. Always fill jars to the top (leave only 1 cm headspace) to reduce air. During transport, keep jars upright and cushioned. Use cardboard dividers or wrap jars in newspaper. Avoid leaving products in a hot vehicle or in direct sun. If youâre transporting in a pickup or lorry, cover the load with a light-coloured tarpaulin to reflect heat. Try to travel in the cooler hours of the morning or evening. For display, keep products out of direct sunlight. A shaded stall or a table under an umbrella is better than an open sunny spot. If you have a refrigerator or cooler, use it for display, but many small vendors donât. In that case, rotate stock: sell older jars first. Keep a record of production dates and check jars daily for signs of spoilage. If you see a bulging lid or mould, remove that jar immediately so it doesnât contaminate others. Also, keep the display area clean and dry. Dust and flies can introduce microbes. Use a clean cloth to wipe jars. If you sell opened jars for immediate use, keep them in a cooler with ice packs. For long-distance transport, consider vacuum-sealing jars or using oxygen absorbers, but these add cost. The simplest rule: keep it cool, keep it clean, keep it covered. With these practices, you can reduce spoilage losses by half or more, meaning more profit and happier customers.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Preservation and Shelf Life for Tomato Paste & Sauce

For a tomato paste or sauce business, shelf life is not a technical footnote â it is the difference between repeat customers and a ruined reputation. A jar of sauce that spoils on a shop shelf, or a bucket of paste that develops mould in a distributor's store, destroys trust and cash flow at the same time. This module gives you the practical numbers, tests and habits you need to protect your product from the kitchen to the customer's hand.

Tomato products are acidic (pH typically 3.5â4.6) and high in moisture, which makes them a target for spoilage yeasts, moulds and acid-tolerant bacteria. Your job is to control the three things that determine shelf life: heat, acidity and hygiene. Get these right and you can sell safely for months; get them wrong and spoilage can appear in days.

Lesson 1: Why Tomato Products Spoil â Mould, Yeast and Bacteria

Spoilage is simply micro-organisms finding food, moisture and warmth. Tomato paste and sauce provide all three. Moulds grow on the surface where air meets product â the classic green or black fuzz on an opened jar. Yeasts ferment sugars and produce gas, alcohol and off-flavours; they tolerate acid well, so they thrive in tomato products. Bacteria cause souring, slime and gas; some, like Clostridium botulinum, are dangerous in low-acid conditions, though tomato's natural acidity usually prevents this if pH is below 4.6.

The practical lesson for African processors: spoilage almost always starts with a hygiene failure â dirty equipment, unwashed hands, contaminated water, or a jar that was not properly sealed or heated. Control the source and you control the shelf life.

Lesson 2: Using Heat Processing to Extend Shelf Life

Heat is your most powerful tool. For tomato sauce in glass jars, a hot-fill-and-hold or water-bath process at 85â95Â°C for 15â30 minutes (depending on jar size) pasteurises the product and creates a partial vacuum as it cools. For paste, the concentration step itself (evaporation at 85â100Â°C) reduces water activity, which slows spoilage. The key is to fill hot, seal immediately, and invert the jar for 2â5 minutes so the hot product sterilises the lid.

Table 1: Recommended heat treatment and target shelf life for tomato products (small-scale processing)
ProductProcessTarget pHExpected shelf life (unopened, cool dark storage)
Tomato sauce (glass jar, 500ml)Hot fill 90Â°C, invert 3 min, cool<4.26â12 months
Tomato paste (glass jar, 500ml)Hot fill 90Â°C, invert 3 min, cool<4.29â18 months
Tomato sauce (plastic pouch)Hot fill 85Â°C, seal, cool<4.23â6 months
Tomato paste (bulk bucket, 5kg)Hot fill 90Â°C, seal, cool<4.23â6 months (once opened: 5â7 days refrigerated)

Source: Adapted from FAO, Small-scale Fruit and Vegetable Processing (FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin 119, 1995) and ITC/UNCTAD, Manual on the Preservation of Fruit and Vegetables.

Lesson 3: Natural Preservatives â Lemon Juice, Vinegar and Salt

Acid, salt and sugar are the oldest preservatives in Africa and remain the most affordable. Lemon juice and vinegar lower pH, making the product hostile to bacteria. Salt reduces water activity and inhibits many spoilage organisms. A practical rule: aim for a final pH below 4.2. Use 1â2 tablespoons of lemon juice or 1 tablespoon of vinegar per 500ml of sauce, then check with a pH strip or meter. Salt at 1.5â2% of product weight also improves flavour and safety.

Table 2: Natural preservative doses and their effect on tomato products
PreservativeTypical dose (per 500ml sauce)EffectNotes
Lemon juice (fresh or bottled)1â2 tbsp (15â30ml)Lowers pH; inhibits bacteriaAdd at end of cooking to preserve flavour
Vinegar (5% acetic acid)1 tbsp (15ml)Lowers pH; inhibits yeasts and mouldsUse white or apple cider vinegar
Salt7.5â10g (1.5â2%)Reduces water activity; inhibits bacteriaDo not exceed 2% for taste
Sugar (optional)1â2 tspBinds water; improves tasteHigh sugar alone is not enough for safety

Source: FAO, Guidelines for the Preservation of Fruit and Vegetables (1995); WHO, Five Keys to Safer Food Manual (2006).

â  SAFETY WARNING â BOTULISM RISK

Never sell or taste a jar that is bulging, leaking, or has an off-smell. Clostridium botulinum can grow in low-acid tomato products and produces a deadly toxin with no visible mould. If pH is above 4.6, you must use a pressure canner or add acid to bring pH below 4.6. When in doubt, throw it out â never "just boil it and sell it".

Lesson 4: Proper Cooling and Storage After Opening

Once a jar is opened, the clock starts. Air, moisture and ambient heat allow yeasts and moulds to grow quickly. The rule for African markets: refrigerate after opening if you have reliable power; if not, keep in the coolest, darkest place and consume within 3â5 days. For bulk paste sold to restaurants, decant into clean, dry containers and cover with a thin layer of oil to exclude air.

Storage temperature matters enormously. Every 10Â°C rise roughly doubles spoilage speed. A jar that lasts 12 months at 20Â°C may last only 3â4 months at 35Â°C. In hot African climates, shade, ventilation and insulated boxes are not luxuries â they are business tools.

Lesson 5: Testing Shelf Life Without a Laboratory

You do not need a lab to run a basic shelf-life test. Keep a "control sample" from each batch, label it with date and batch number, and store it under the same conditions as your stock. Check it every week for:

  • Smell: any sour, alcoholic or "off" odour.
  • Look: surface film, bubbles, colour change, mould spots.
  • Texture: slime, gas pockets, separation that will not mix back.
  • Packaging: bulging lids, leaks, rust.

Record results in a simple notebook. After 3â6 months you will know your real shelf life and can print an honest "best before" date. This is also powerful for buyers â it shows you are professional.

Lesson 6: Reducing Spoilage During Transport and Display

Most losses happen after the factory gate. In transport, avoid stacking in direct sun, use covered vehicles, and pack jars so they cannot knock together and crack seals. For display, rotate stock (first in, first out), keep products off the floor and away from walls, and never place jars in direct sunlight or next to a generator or oven. In open markets, use a shaded stall and sell from sealed containers. Train your sellers to check seals and dates daily.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Check pH of every batch â target below 4.2; record it.
  2. Hot fill at 85â95Â°C and invert sealed jars for 2â5 minutes.
  3. Use clean, dry, undamaged jars and new lids every time.
  4. Add lemon juice, vinegar or salt to control pH and water activity.
  5. Cool jars quickly on a clean rack, not in cold water.
  6. Label every batch with date and batch number; keep a control sample.
  7. Store in a cool, dark, dry place; refrigerate after opening.
  8. Train transporters and sellers to protect seals and rotate stock.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Small-scale Fruit and Vegetable Processing (Agricultural Services Bulletin 119)
  • WHO â Five Keys to Safer Food Manual
  • FAO â Manual on the Preservation of Fruit and Vegetables
  • FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius â Codes of Practice (Canned Foods)
  • USDA â Home Canning Guides (free, practical heat-processing reference)

Business bottom line: every jar you save from spoilage is profit you keep. Invest in a pH meter, clean jars, a thermometer and a shaded store. Your customers will taste the difference â and come back.

quiz.q: What are the three main types of microorganisms that spoil tomato products?
quiz.explanation: Moulds, yeasts, and bacteria are the primary spoilage organisms in tomato products.

quiz.q: Which condition speeds up spoilage of tomato sauce?
quiz.explanation: High humidity, especially with warmth, promotes microbial growth.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of heat processing?
options: B) To kill spoilage organisms and seal the product
quiz.explanation: Heat processing kills microbes and creates a seal to prevent recontamination.

quiz.q: How long should you boil pint jars of tomato sauce in a hot water bath?
quiz.explanation: Pint jars require 35â45 minutes of boiling water processing for safety.

quiz.q: What should you do if a jar lid does not seal after processing?
options: C) Refrigerate and use within a week
quiz.explanation: An unsealed jar is not shelf-stable and must be refrigerated and used quickly.

quiz.q: Which natural preservative lowers pH to prevent microbial growth?
quiz.explanation: Lemon juice contains acid that lowers pH, inhibiting spoilage organisms.

quiz.q: How much bottled lemon juice should you add per 500 ml of tomato sauce for safety?
quiz.explanation: One tablespoon of bottled lemon juice per 500 ml ensures adequate acidity.

quiz.q: What is the maximum pH for safe shelf storage of tomato products?
quiz.explanation: A pH of 4.6 or lower prevents the growth of dangerous bacteria like Clostridium botulinum.

quiz.q: How does salt help preserve tomato paste?
options: B) It draws water out of microbes
quiz.explanation: Salt dehydrates microbes, slowing or stopping their growth.

quiz.q: After opening a jar of tomato sauce, how long can it be kept in the refrigerator?
quiz.explanation: Opened tomato sauce can be refrigerated for 7â10 days for best quality.

quiz.q: What should you do with leftover tomato paste to extend its life?
options: A) Leave it in the jar at room temperature
B) Freeze it in ice cube trays
quiz.explanation: Freezing in small portions allows you to thaw only what you need, reducing waste.

quiz.q: Why should you not eat food from a jar with a bulging lid?
options: B) It means the product is too acidic
C) It shows the product is fresh
D) It is a sign of high sugar
quiz.explanation: A bulging lid is a sign of microbial gas production, often from spoilage bacteria.

quiz.q: Which sense can help you detect spoilage without a lab?
quiz.explanation: Smell can detect off-odours like alcohol or rot, indicating spoilage.

quiz.q: What does a fizzy or bubbly appearance in tomato sauce indicate?
quiz.explanation: Bubbles are a sign of yeast fermentation, which spoils the product.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for active spoilage using a spoon?
options: A) Leave a spoonful in a covered glass for 24 hours
D) Add salt to the spoon
quiz.explanation: If bubbles or bad smell develop after 24 hours, spoilage is active.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid direct sunlight during transport and display?
options: B) It speeds up spoilage by heating the product
C) It changes the colour only
quiz.explanation: Sunlight raises temperature, accelerating microbial growth and spoilage.

quiz.q: What is the best way to pack jars for transport?
options: B) Wrap in newspaper and keep upright
C) Lay them on their sides
D) Put them in direct sun
quiz.explanation: Cushioning and keeping jars upright prevents breakage and leakage.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see mould on the surface of tomato paste?
options: A) Scrape it off and eat the rest
B) Throw away the whole jar
quiz.explanation: Mould roots may extend deep, so the entire product is unsafe.

quiz.q: How can you reduce spoilage during display at a market?
options: A) Keep jars in direct sun
B) Rotate stock and keep area clean
D) Stack jars in a hot place
quiz.explanation: Rotating stock and maintaining cleanliness reduce contamination and spoilage.

quiz.q: What is a sign that a jar of tomato sauce has spoiled?
quiz.explanation: A bulging lid indicates gas production by spoilage organisms.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a natural preservative for tomato products?
quiz.explanation: Sugar is not typically used as a preservative for tomato products; it can even promote spoilage.

quiz.q: What is the correct headspace to leave when filling jars for heat processing?
quiz.explanation: 1â2 cm headspace allows for expansion and proper sealing during processing.

quiz.q: How can you tell if a jar has sealed properly after heat processing?
options: B) The centre of the lid is firm and does not move
quiz.explanation: A sealed lid is concave and firm; if it pops, it's not sealed.

quiz.q: Why is it important to use bottled lemon juice instead of fresh for preserving?
quiz.explanation: Bottled lemon juice has a standardized pH, ensuring reliable acidity.

quiz.q: What should you do before filling jars with tomato product?
quiz.explanation: Sterilising jars kills existing microbes, preventing contamination.

quiz.q: How long can frozen tomato paste be kept?
quiz.explanation: Frozen tomato paste maintains quality for 3â6 months.

quiz.q: What is a sign of yeast spoilage in tomato sauce?
quiz.explanation: Yeasts produce alcohol and carbon dioxide, causing an alcoholic smell.

quiz.q: How can you test the pH of your tomato product without a lab?
quiz.explanation: Inexpensive pH strips give a rough measure of acidity.

quiz.q: What is the recommended processing time for quart jars of tomato sauce in a boiling water bath?
quiz.explanation: Quart jars need 45â55 minutes due to their larger volume.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid double-dipping into a jar of tomato paste?
options: B) It introduces microbes from your mouth
D) It makes it too salty
quiz.explanation: Double-dipping transfers bacteria from your mouth into the product, speeding spoilage.
